item.title: Re: makes sense
item.content:encoded:
There's actually an interesting examination of potential ways to create an artificial blackhole in the original research paper that served as an inspiration for this. The basic idea comes down to firing a hell of a lot of lasers at the same point at once, and hoping that the energy of all those photons in a single place will collapse into a blackhole. The science checks out (at least at the moment; developments in quantum gravity theory might change that), the main issue is just constructing and powering that many lasers in deep space.

Interesting thing though: once you have one black hole, making more of them becomes a lot easier, because you can use the hawking radiation of the black hole to convert mass into energy at 100% efficiency (minus whatever losses are involved in your collection apparatus). And this will work with any matter you throw into the thing. Even garbage. So you've now got a way to turn any waste material directly into energy, and that energy can be used to power another black hole generator.

Congratulations!

Here's to many more awesome GOI formats in years to come.

item.title: Author Post
item.content:encoded:
Most of this proposal is entirely plausible under current physics, if many hundreds of years beyond our current tech level. For those curious about the finer details of constructing a black hole powered starship, I refer you to this paper, which was an invaluable reference during the writing of this article. It's a shame that I couldn't use it as one of the citations in-universe due to its publishing date in 2009.

The object accelerating towards Earth, PSR B0531+21, is SCP-1548 a skip that no longer exists.

Thanks go out to the following people for helping critique and review this: TyGently, TwistedGears, Decibelles, Doctor Cimmerian, minmin, Dr Leonard, Randomini, tahunu, Dr Gravity, MrWrong, sirpudding, and various other members of #site19. If I missed your name, feel free to give me a poke and I'll add you to the list.

The diagram used for Figure A is my own work, which I am releasing under CC-BY-SA 3.0. It was created as a .svg in Inkscape, and then exported as a .png.
